elements.name: Command
elements.what: Reify a request or action as a first-class object that can be stored, passed around, executed, undone, and replayed.
elements.problem: Decouples the invoker of an operation from the operation itself; enables undo/redo, input remapping, command queues, and replay/demo recording.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: Flyweight
elements.what: Share a single instance of intrinsic (context-independent) state among many logical objects, keeping extrinsic state outside the shared part.
elements.problem: Thousands of fine-grained objects (trees, tiles, glyphs) duplicate identical heavy data; sharing the common part cuts memory and enables techniques like instanced rendering.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: Observer
elements.what: A subject maintains a list of observers and notifies them automatically when its state changes.
elements.problem: One-to-many dependency between objects without coupling the subject to concrete dependents (e.g. achievements reacting to gameplay events).
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: Prototype
elements.what: Create new objects by cloning a prototypical instance rather than instantiating a class.
elements.problem: Object kinds must be definable and composable at runtime (spawners, data-driven entity definitions) without a parallel explosion of classes or spawner types.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: Singleton
elements.what: Ensure a class has exactly one instance and provide a global access point to it.
elements.problem: Some services genuinely need a single shared instance; the pattern gives controlled, lazy access to it (Nystrom's chapter is largely a caution against overuse, offering alternatives).
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: State
elements.what: Represent each state of an object as a separate object/class and delegate state-dependent behavior to the current state object.
elements.problem: Behavior that varies by mode (character movement, AI, menus) degenerates into tangles of conditionals; explicit state objects make transitions and per-state behavior tractable (OO realization of a finite state machine).
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: Double Buffer
elements.what: Maintain two copies of a piece of state - one being read/displayed while the other is written - and swap them atomically when the write completes.
elements.problem: A consumer must never observe state mid-modification (torn frames, half-updated simulation state); writing into a hidden buffer and swapping makes updates appear instantaneous.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Game Loop
elements.what: A continuous loop that processes input without blocking, updates the simulation, and renders, decoupling the progression of game time from user input and processor speed.
elements.problem: Interactive simulations must keep running at a controlled rate regardless of whether the user does anything and regardless of hardware speed; the loop owns time and drives everything else.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Update Method
elements.what: Simulate a collection of independent objects by giving each an update() method that the game loop calls once per frame, letting each object advance its own behavior one step at a time.
elements.problem: Many active entities must appear to behave concurrently; per-frame incremental updates avoid one object monopolizing control while keeping each object's behavior encapsulated.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Bytecode
elements.what: Encode behavior as instructions for a small purpose-built virtual machine and execute it with an interpreter, instead of hard-coding it in the host language.
elements.problem: Behavior must be data-driven, moddable, hot-reloadable, or sandboxed; native code is too rigid and privileged, while Interpreter-pattern object trees are too slow and memory-hungry.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Subclass Sandbox
elements.what: A base class defines an abstract sandbox method and a suite of protected operations; subclasses implement their behavior by combining only those provided operations.
elements.problem: Many similar subclasses (e.g. dozens of superpowers) would each couple to many game systems; funneling all their behavior through base-class primitives confines coupling to one place.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Type Object
elements.what: Represent a category of things as an ordinary runtime object (the type object) that instances hold a reference to, instead of as a compile-time class.
elements.problem: New kinds of entities (monster breeds, item types) must be definable in data without recompiling or growing a class hierarchy; type-as-data makes kinds authorable and shareable at runtime.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Component
elements.what: Split a single entity's state and behavior across multiple component objects, one per domain (physics, rendering, AI, input), which the entity aggregates.
elements.problem: A monolithic entity class couples every domain together and deep inheritance hierarchies cannot express cross-cutting combinations; composition of per-domain components keeps domains isolated and entities configurable.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Event Queue
elements.what: Decouple when an event or message is sent from when it is processed by storing it in a queue that a receiver drains later.
elements.problem: Sender and receiver must be decoupled in time (and identity): aggregating, deferring, or deduplicating requests (sound playback, tutorial triggers) without the sender blocking on processing.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Service Locator
elements.what: Provide a global access point to a service through a locator that resolves the concrete provider at runtime, hiding both the provider's class and the lookup process.
elements.problem: Code all over the codebase needs a service (audio, logging) without coupling to a concrete implementation or passing it everywhere; the locator centralizes binding and allows swapping providers (including null services) at runtime.
elements.named_in: Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies - Alur, Crupi, Malks (2001)

elements.name: Data Locality
elements.what: Arrange data contiguously in memory in the order it is processed (e.g. packed homogeneous arrays instead of pointer-linked heap objects) to exploit CPU caching.
elements.problem: Memory access dominates modern performance; pointer-chasing scattered objects thrashes the cache, while contiguous hot data turns cache misses into streaming reads.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Dirty Flag
elements.what: Track whether derived data is out of sync with its primary source using a boolean flag, and recompute the derived data only when it is both dirty and needed.
elements.problem: Expensive derived computation (world transforms, saved-state sync) should not rerun on every source change or every read; the flag defers and batches recalculation to the last responsible moment.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Object Pool
elements.what: Preallocate a fixed collection of reusable objects and satisfy allocation requests by recycling inactive members instead of allocating and freeing on the heap.
elements.problem: Frequent creation/destruction of short-lived objects (particles, bullets, audio voices) causes allocation cost and memory fragmentation - fatal on consoles/embedded; pooling bounds memory and makes allocation O(1).
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Spatial Partition
elements.what: Store objects in a data structure organized by their spatial position (grid, quadtree, BSP, etc.) so that location-based queries need only examine nearby cells.
elements.problem: Finding objects near a point or each other (collision, combat range, rendering culling) is O(n^2) by pairwise scan; position-keyed structures cut queries to near-constant or logarithmic cost. Concrete structures (quadtree, k-d tree, BSP) are enumerated in the datastructures corpus, not here.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Entity Component System
elements.what: Organize a simulation as plain-id entities, pure-data components stored in contiguous per-type arrays, and systems that iterate over all entities holding a given component set.
elements.problem: Deep entity class hierarchies cannot express cross-cutting feature combinations and scatter hot data; ECS composes capabilities as data and lets systems process components in cache-friendly batches.
elements.named_in: Evolve Your Hierarchy: Refactoring Game Entities with Components - Mick West (2007)
elements.borderline: In-process program-organization pattern that verges on engine-level architecture; included per charter - it is implementable inside one program, named, and recurring across codebases.

elements.name: Scene Graph
elements.what: Represent a scene as a hierarchy of nodes whose spatial transforms (and other attributes) compose parent-to-child, so moving a parent moves its whole subtree.
elements.problem: Objects are naturally attached to one another (turret on tank, moon around planet); a hierarchy lets local transforms be authored independently while world transforms are derived by composition, and supports hierarchical culling and traversal.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Rendering - Akenine-Moller, Haines, Hoffman (2008, 3rd ed.)

elements.name: Fixed Timestep
elements.what: Advance the simulation in constant-size time increments driven by an accumulator of elapsed real time, decoupling the simulation rate from the (variable) render rate, typically with interpolation of the leftover fraction for display.
elements.problem: Variable delta-time updates make physics non-deterministic, unstable at low frame rates, and irreproducible; a fixed step gives determinism and stability while the accumulator keeps game time synchronized with wall-clock time.
elements.named_in: Fix Your Timestep! - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2004)

elements.name: Dirty Rectangles
elements.what: Track the screen regions modified since the last frame and redraw or recomposite only those rectangles instead of the whole display.
elements.problem: Full-screen redraw wastes time when only small areas change (sprites over static background, UI repaint); region invalidation makes redraw cost proportional to actual change. A regional specialization of the dirty-flag idea, kept separate because the tracked unit (2D regions, merging/overlap handling) is its own mechanism.
elements.named_in: Michael Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book - Michael Abrash (1997), ch. 45 'Dog Hair and Dirty Rectangles'

elements.name: Level of Detail
elements.what: Maintain multiple representations of an object at different fidelities and select the cheapest one whose error is imperceptible given current importance (typically distance from the viewer).
elements.problem: Rendering or simulating everything at full fidelity wastes resources on objects that contribute little to the result; graded representations bound cost while preserving perceived quality. Generalizes beyond graphics (audio, AI, simulation LOD).
elements.named_in: Level of Detail for 3D Graphics - Luebke, Reddy, Cohen, Varshney, Watson, Huebner (2003)
elements.borderline: Graphics-domain optimization technique rather than a general software mechanism, but it is named, recurring, and implementable inside one component; included per charter.

elements.name: Snapshot Interpolation
elements.what: Buffer received snapshots of remote simulation state for a short delay and render by interpolating between two slightly-past snapshots, reconstructing smooth motion from discrete, jittery updates.
elements.problem: State updates arrive at a lower and irregular rate than the display refresh; interpolating between delayed buffered snapshots hides network jitter and packet spacing at the cost of added latency.
elements.named_in: Snapshot Interpolation - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2015)
elements.borderline: A networked-game state-synchronization technique, but the buffering-and-interpolation mechanism itself is implemented entirely inside the receiving process; the surrounding client-server topology is parked for Phase 3.

parked_architecture.name: Authoritative server with client-side prediction
parked_architecture.why: System-level netcode topology (who owns truth, how clients reconcile) - a statement about multi-node structure, not an in-process mechanism; the in-process piece (snapshot interpolation) is cataloged above.

parked_architecture.name: Layered game engine runtime architecture
parked_architecture.why: Gregory-style engine layering (platform/core/resources/gameplay) is whole-system structure; encountered while sourcing scene graph, belongs to the Phase 3 architecture realm.

excluded_notable.name: Per-frame / frame arena allocator (single-frame allocator)
excluded_notable.why: Folded as aka of memory arena per charter (arena owned by the resource-management sweep); naming source for the game-specific form: 'Frame-Based Memory Allocation' - Steven Ranck, Game Programming Gems 1 (2000). Central merge should attach these aliases and source to the arena element.

excluded_notable.name: Data-oriented design
excluded_notable.why: A design philosophy/methodology broader than any single mechanism; its concrete cacheable-layout mechanism is captured as the Data Locality element.

excluded_notable.name: Variable timestep / delta-time update
excluded_notable.why: Recorded as a variation inside the Game Loop chapter rather than a separate element; the established named mechanism in this space is Fixed Timestep, cataloged separately.

notes: Coverage: all 19 Game Programming Patterns chapters confirmed against the live ToC at gameprogrammingpatterns.com/contents.html this session (Design Patterns Revisited 6, Sequencing 3, Behavioral 3, Decoupling 3, Optimization 4) - none missed. Decisions: (1) Fixed Timestep kept SEPARATE from Game Loop: it has its own canonical naming source (Fiedler 2004), and its mechanism (accumulator decoupling simulation step size from render rate, with render interpolation) is distinct from the loop structure itself; Nystrom's Game Loop chapter covers it only as a variation. (2) The six GoF revisits cite GoF (corpus id 'gof') as naming source and carry tag 'gof-revisit' - central merge should dedup them against the GoF scout's entries. (3) Event Queue lists 'message queue (in-process)' as aka - flag for central merge against any messaging-scout element. (4) Dirty Rectangles kept separate from Dirty Flag (region-tracking mechanism vs boolean invalidation), with the relation noted in its problem field. (5) Spatial Partition kept at role granularity; quadtree/BSP/k-d variants deliberately not enumerated (datastructures corpus territory). (6) Service Locator's naming source is Core J2EE Patterns (2001), predating both Fowler's 2004 article and Nystrom. (7) ECS, LOD, and Snapshot Interpolation included with borderline tags per charter. Nystrom's book is NOT in the corpus work-id map (grep confirmed) - Phase 2 should add it as a new node. Thin spots: PLoP-era game pattern papers (Bjork & Holopainen 'Patterns in Game Design' is game *design*, not software mechanisms - deliberately not swept); Game Programming Gems series only touched for the frame-allocator note and likely names more mechanisms (e.g. object caching variants) - a Gems sweep could add a handful more.
